provenance.note: Measured at load 1.98 after the NCC hot-loop change (b1d74bf): four accumulator chains in prepare_chip! and integral_both!, ifelse for the denominator guard, FFTW_PATIENT plans. This run carries the CPU-time column, which exists because two earlier readings of this table were wrong without it. Wall clock is work divided by parallelism achieved; CPU time is the work. On a shared machine only the latter is comparable across runs. The change is a real win at both thread counts, from an interleaved A/B against its parent b4fb528 -- two reps, alternating base/HEAD so a load spike cannot land on one side, identical 920544 points: 1 thread 75.6 -> 68.6 s CPU (9.3% less work, wall 74.1 -> 67.0), 12 threads 89.7 -> 82.2 s CPU (8.4% less, wall 22.2 -> 21.6). Both reproduce to within 0.3 s. Two retracted claims, recorded so neither is re-derived. First: that the 12-thread wall clock (33-35 s at load 2.7-3.5) was contention. Second: that a non-interleaved A/B showed the change 1.03x SLOWER threaded. The first was right in substance and dismissed too early; the second was the artifact -- its base and HEAD runs were not interleaved, so a load spike biased one side. At load 1.98 this row is 21.3 s at 3.83 cores, faster than the 8d7c1ec run's 25.6 s, so the ~2.85 cores seen at higher load was the machine and not a lost-parallelism regression. The 4096 lazy row peaked at 9537 MiB against 3599 at 2048: 25 blocks on 12 threads holds twelve 6144-pixel working sets at once, which measures the block size being large relative to the scene rather than what blocking costs. 8192 is excluded for the same reason at 9 blocks. Column set reduced afterwards: `cores used` is dropped, being CPU time over runtime, and the thread count moved into the configuration label. Rows group by implementation rather than sorting purely by runtime, which interleaved the three and separated the comparisons a reader wants. The `group` fields and thread-annotated labels in this file were backfilled onto the load-1.98 measurements rather than re-measured -- a relabel, no timing changed -- because the machine was at load 4.4 by then and re-running the threaded rows there is exactly the error the CPU-time column exists to prevent. The python row's 417 s CPU against 180 s wall was checked rather than trusted, since an inflated CPU-to-wall ratio is usually a spinning thread pool. It is not: OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive moves user time 0.3% (406.7 s against 405.3), and OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 takes 374.5 s wall for 370.9 s user -- so the parallel run's user time is genuine parallel work, only ~9% above the serial total, spread over ~2.3 cores. All three runs return the same 2791308 points. The reference therefore costs ~5x AutoRIFT.jl's CPU time (417 s against 81.6), which is a larger gap than the 8.5x in wall clock is usually read as, and it scales poorly on its own terms: 1 thread to default is 374.5 s to 180.4.
